  - Avoid using PowerShell to run commands that have dedicated tools, unless explicitly instructed:
    - File search: Use Glob (NOT Get-ChildItem -Recurse)
    - Content search: Use Grep (NOT Select-String)
    - Read files: Use Read (NOT Get-Content)
    - Edit files: Use Edit
    - Write files: Use Write (NOT Set-Content/Out-File)
    - Communication: Output text directly (NOT Write-Output/Write-Host)
  - When issuing multiple commands:
    - If the commands are independent and can run in parallel, make multiple PowerShell tool calls in a single message.
    - If the commands depend on each other and must run sequentially, chain them in a single PowerShell call (see edition-specific chaining syntax above).
    - Use `;` only when you need to run commands sequentially but don't care if earlier commands fail.
    - DO NOT use newlines to separate commands (newlines are ok in quoted strings and here-strings)
  - Do NOT prefix commands with `cd` or `Set-Location` -- the working directory is already set to the correct project directory automatically.
  - Avoid unnecessary `Start-Sleep` commands:
    - Do not sleep between commands that can run immediately — just run them.
    - If your command is long running and you would like to be notified when it finishes — simply run your command using `run_in_background`. There is no need to sleep in this case.
    - Do not retry failing commands in a sleep loop — diagnose the root cause or consider an alternative approach.
    - If waiting for a background task you started with `run_in_background`, you will be notified when it completes — do not poll.
    - If you must poll an external process, use a check command rather than sleeping first.
    - If you must sleep, keep the duration short to avoid blocking the user.
  - For git commands:
    - Prefer to create a new commit rather than amending an existing commit.
    - Before running destructive operations (e.g., git reset --hard, git push --force, git checkout --), consider whether there is a safer alternative that achieves the same goal. Only use destructive operations when they are truly the best approach.
    - Never skip hooks (--no-verify) or bypass signing (--no-gpg-sign, -c commit.gpgsign=false) unless the user has explicitly asked for it. If a hook fails, investigate and fix the underlying issue.

timeout.description: Optional timeout in milliseconds (max 600000 for a foreground command)

description.description: Clear, concise description of what this command does in active voice.

run_in_background.description: Set to true to run this command in the background.

dangerouslyDisableSandbox.description: Set this to true to dangerously override sandbox mode and run commands without sandboxing.

tools.name: Read
tools.description:
Reads a file from the local filesystem.

- `file_path` must be an absolute path.
- Reads up to 2000 lines by default.
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- Reads images (PNG, JPG, …) and presents them visually. Reads PDFs via the `pages` parameter (e.g. "1-5", max 20 pages/request; required for PDFs over 10 pages). Reads Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb) as cells with outputs.
- Reading a directory, a missing file, or an empty file returns an error or system reminder rather than content.
- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

file_path.description: The absolute path to the file to read

offset.description: The line number to start reading from. Only provide if the file is too large to read at once

limit.description: The number of lines to read. Only provide if the file is too large to read at once.

pages.description: Page range for PDF files (e.g., "1-5", "3", "10-20"). Only applicable to PDF files. Maximum 20 pages per request.

allow_large.description: Set to true to read a text file, or a line range of one, that is over the usual size limits, up to what still fits in your context. Only use this when you genuinely need all of it or the user asked for the whole file; otherwise read it in parts with offset and limit, or search it.

tools.name: ReportFindings
tools.description: Report code-review findings as a typed list so the host UI can render them. Use this only when the active code-review instructions tell you to report findings with this tool; otherwise follow whatever output format those instructions specify. When reporting a review's results, call it once with the verified findings ranked most-severe first (empty array if nothing survived verification) and do not also print the findings as text. When re-reporting after applying fixes (only if the apply instructions ask for it), set `outcome` on each finding to what actually happened.

level.description: Effort level the review ran at

findings.description: Verified findings, most-severe first; empty if none survived

file.description: Repo-relative path of the file the finding is in

short_summary.description: Compressed label for compact UI (≤60 chars): the claim alone, no rationale or consequence clause

category.description: Short kebab-case slug of the finding type, e.g. "correctness", "simplification", "efficiency", "test-coverage"

verdict.description: Set when a verify pass ran; absent on inline-only reviews

outcome.description: Set ONLY when re-reporting after applying fixes: what happened to this finding

tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

delaySeconds.description: Seconds from now to wake up. Clamped to [60, 3600] by the runtime. Required unless `stop` is true.

reason.description: One short sentence explaining the chosen delay. Goes to telemetry and is shown to the user. Be specific. Required unless `stop` is true.

prompt.description: The /loop input to fire on wake-up. Pass the same /loop input verbatim each turn so the next firing re-enters the skill and continues the loop. For autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` instead (the dynamic-pacing variant, not the CronCreate-mode `<<autonomous-loop>>`). Required unless `stop` is true.

stop.description: Set to true to end the dynamic loop immediately instead of scheduling another wakeup. When true, all other fields are ignored and no further wakeups fire.

noop.description: true = nothing changed (you checked and there is nothing to report). false = something happened worth keeping (edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, surfaced a finding). Consecutive noop:true ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak. Required unless `stop` is true.

tools.name: SendFeedback
tools.description:
Use this tool to draft feedback about Claude Code when you hit a high-signal moment. That includes both PRODUCT issues and MODEL-BEHAVIOR issues:
- a reproducible tool or product failure was just resolved or abandoned
- the user clearly expressed frustration with Claude Code or with how you handled the task
- you hit a missing capability that blocked a reasonable request
- you notice, or the user points out, that your own behavior in this session went wrong, for example: you gave a confident answer then had to retract it; you stopped short and handed work back when you could have finished; you declined or disputed a reasonable request; you spawned more subagents than the task warranted; your tone was off; you asked more clarifying questions than needed; you expanded scope beyond what was asked

The draft is QUEUED LOCALLY. It is never sent without the user's explicit approval, and calling this tool renders no UI and does not interrupt the conversation, so never announce it or ask the user about it mid-task.

Write `details` as short labeled bullets in this exact order, one to three lines each, no narrative paragraphs:
- **What happened:** the observed behavior vs. what was expected, with exact error text if short. Facts only.
- **What the user said:** the user's own words that prompted this, quoted. If nothing did, write "User didn't comment; observed by the model." Never paraphrase sentiment into a stronger claim.
- **Repro:** the minimal steps or shape that reproduces it.
- **Evidence:** identifiers a reader can chase, such as request IDs, timestamps, file paths, versions. Omit the bullet if there are none.

Constraints:
- Never fabricate or exaggerate user sentiment; report only what actually happened.
- Everything in the draft must be sourced from the user or the session, never inferred: leave unknown fields blank rather than guess, and add a final **Cause:** bullet only for a root cause you verified in-session.
- Use `area` to name the part of Claude Code the feedback is about (a feature, command, or workflow, e.g. "hooks config", "/help", "file editing") when there is a clear one; leave it blank otherwise.
- Use `failure_mode` ONLY when the report is about model behavior (how Claude responded), not a product bug. Pick the single closest value, or `other` when it is a model-behavior issue that fits no listed value; omit the field only when the report is a product/tool bug with no model-behavior component.
- Use `task_category` to name what kind of task the session was doing, or `other` when it is a clear task that fits no listed value. Omit only if genuinely unclear.
- Do not include secrets or credentials. Refer to people by role ("a teammate", "the PR reviewer"), never by name, email address, or chat/user ID. This applies inside quoted user words too: replace a name or handle with a bracketed role (e.g. "[a teammate]") and keep the rest verbatim. Do not include customer-facing channel or DM IDs, or excerpts of customer content. Session, request, and run IDs, timestamps, repo/PR numbers, and file paths (written relative to the working directory, or ~-prefixed, not absolute paths under the user's home) remain the right evidence.
- If the issue looks like a security vulnerability: describe the class of problem, never a working exploit or step-by-step extraction path.
- Draft only at the natural moments listed above, and at most one draft per distinct issue; never re-draft the same issue in a session.

type.description: What kind of feedback this is.

title.description: Short, specific one-line summary of the issue.

details.description: Labeled bullets, in order: **What happened:** (observed vs. expected, exact error text if short); **What the user said:** (quoted, or "User didn't comment; observed by the model."); **Repro:** (minimal steps); **Evidence:** (request IDs, timestamps, paths, versions; omit if none); optionally a final **Cause:** only if verified in-session. One to three lines per bullet. No narrative paragraphs, no speculation, no secrets.

area.description: Optional short tag naming the part of Claude Code this is about (e.g. "hooks config", "/help", "file editing"). Leave blank if unclear.

failure_mode.description: When the report is about MODEL BEHAVIOR (not a product bug), the closest failure mode, or `other` when it is a model-behavior issue that fits no listed value. Omit only when the report is a product/tool bug with no model-behavior component.

task_category.description: What kind of task the session was doing when the issue occurred, or `other` when it is a clear task that fits no listed value. Omit only if genuinely unclear.

tools.name: SendMessage
tools.description:
# SendMessage

Send a message to another agent.

```json
{"to": "researcher", "summary": "assign task 1", "message": "start on task #1"}
```

| `to` | |
|---|---|
| `"researcher"` | Teammate by name |
| `"main"` | The main conversation (background subagents only) |
| `"worker"` | Any agent from `ListAgents` — subagent, another local Claude session |
| `"worker [3fa9c1]"` | Same, plus its `[ref]` — only when a listing or an error shows one |

Your plain text output is NOT visible to other agents — to communicate, you MUST call this tool. Messages from teammates are delivered automatically; you don't check an inbox. Refer to agents by name — names keep working after an agent completes (a send resumes it from its transcript). Use the raw `agentId` (format `a...-...`) from its spawn result only when the agent has no name, or when a newer agent took the name (latest wins). When relaying, don't quote the original — it's already rendered to the user.

## Cross-session

Use `ListAgents` to discover targets. Every row leads with the agent's `name [ref]` — the name IS the address; there is no separate address syntax.

```json
{"to": "worker", "message": "check if tests pass over there"}
{"to": "worker [3fa9c1]", "message": "you, specifically"}
```

Send the bare name — a name that exactly matches one live agent or session (on this machine, on another machine, or in the cloud) delivers directly. Append the ` [ref]` only when the bare name is not enough — `ListAgents` shows two rows with it, or an error asks you to disambiguate (you typed only a prefix, or a session list could not be checked). A ref you did not just read from a listing or an error will not resolve, and if the same name also names an in-process agent, the bare name always wins — use the in-process one.

A listed peer is alive and will receive your message; messages enqueue and drain at the receiver's next tool round (its `ListAgents` row says whether it is busy or idle right now). A successful send means the message reached that session, not that its Claude read it: a session running in a different permission mode than yours holds cross-session messages for its user's approval (and may let them expire), and a session can refuse them outright — for a session on this machine a `[Cross-session delivery notice]` tells you when that happens (the tool result says when this session has no inbox for one to reach); for a Remote Control, cloud or Claude Desktop session nothing reports back, so never treat silence as agreement. Your message arrives wrapped as `<cross-session-message from="...">`. **To reply to an incoming message, copy its `from` attribute as your `to`.** Cross-session messages travel between SESSIONS: if you are a subagent, your send goes out under your parent session's address, and any reply is delivered to the parent session's conversation, not to you. The receiver reads your message literally in every case (idle or busy, on this machine, over Remote Control or headless): an `@` followed by a file path, or `@server:resource`, attaches nothing there, unlike in your own user's input. So never rely on `@` to deliver content: send the text itself, or a file with its own tool.

To hear when a session ON THIS MACHINE finishes what it is doing, pass `notify_when_idle: true` (from the main conversation only) — one-shot and opt-in: exactly one `[Cross-session idle notice]` arrives when it next goes idle (or exits) — shown to you, or only to your user when this session holds peer messages for approval (the tool result says which); if it never signals within the subscription's lifetime (it may still be busy, may refuse inbound requests, or may have ended abruptly) the notice says the subscription expired instead. Omit `message` for a pure subscription that costs that session nothing; include one to deliver it now AND subscribe. Never poll `ListAgents` in a loop or send "are you done?" messages instead.

Permission boundaries are per-session: NEVER ask a peer to perform an action that was denied or blocked in your session, or that you expect your own permission settings would block — a peer doing it for you bypasses the user's permission decision (cross-session permission laundering). Route blocked work back to your user instead.

to.description: Recipient: a name from ListAgents (append its " [ref]" only when a listing or an error shows one), a teammate name, "main", or a background agent's agentId

summary.description: A 5-10 word label for your own transcript row (not transmitted — the recipient previews the first line of `message`). Truncated to 200 characters rather than rejected.

message.description: Plain text message content. The recipient's human sees only the FIRST LINE as a one-line preview until they expand it, so make the first line a clear, self-contained sentence saying what this is about — not a greeting, preamble, or bare @-mention.

notify_when_idle.description: Ask a session ON THIS MACHINE to send you ONE notice when it next goes idle (finishes its turn with nothing queued) or exits — opt-in, one-shot, no polling. With a message: deliver it now AND subscribe. Without a message (omit it): a pure subscription that costs the other session nothing.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

skill.description: The name of a skill from the available-skills list. Do not guess names.

tools.name: TaskStop
tools.description:
- Stops a running background task by its ID
- Takes a task_id parameter identifying the task to stop
- To stop an agent-team teammate, pass its agent ID or bare teammate name as task_id
- To stop a background agent spawned with a name, pass that name as task_id
- Returns a success or failure status
- Use this tool when you need to terminate a long-running task

task_id.description: The ID of the background task to stop. Agent-team teammates and named background agents are also accepted by agent ID or name.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

query.description: Query to find deferred tools. Use "select:<tool_name>" for direct selection, or keywords to search.

max_results.description: Maximum number of results to return (default: 5)

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

script.description: Self-contained workflow script. Must begin with `export const meta = { name, description, phases }` (pure literal, no computed values) followed by the script body using agent()/parallel()/pipeline()/phase().

name.description: Name of a predefined workflow (built-in or from .claude/workflows/). Resolves to a self-contained script.

description.description: Ignored — set the workflow description in the script's `meta` block.

title.description: Ignored — set the workflow title in the script's `meta` block.

args.description: Optional input value exposed to the script as the global `args`, verbatim. Pass arrays/objects as actual JSON values, NOT as a JSON-encoded string — a stringified list breaks `args.filter`/`args.map` in the script. Use for parameterized named workflows (e.g. a research question).

scriptPath.description: Path to a workflow script file on disk. Every Workflow invocation persists its script under the session directory and returns the path in the tool result. To iterate, edit that file with Write/Edit and re-invoke Workflow with the same `scriptPath` instead of re-sending the full script. Takes precedence over `script` and `name`.

resumeFromRunId.description: Run ID of a prior Workflow invocation to resume from. Completed agent() calls with unchanged (prompt, opts) return their cached results instantly; only edited or new calls re-run. Same-session only. Stop the prior run first (TaskStop) before resuming.

tools.name: Write
tools.description:
Writes a file to the local filesystem, overwriting if one exists.

When to use: creating a new file, or fully replacing one you've already Read. Overwriting an existing file you haven't Read will fail. For partial changes, use Edit instead.

file_path.description: The absolute path to the file to write (must be absolute, not relative)

content.description: The content to write to the file

tools.name: mcp__claude-in-chrome__computer
tools.description:
Use a mouse and keyboard to interact with a web browser, and take screenshots. If you don't have a valid tab ID, use tabs_context_mcp first to get available tabs.
* Whenever you intend to click on an element like an icon, you should consult a screenshot to determine the coordinates of the element before moving the cursor.
* If you tried clicking on a program or link but it failed to load, even after waiting, try adjusting your click location so that the tip of the cursor visually falls on the element that you want to click.
* Make sure to click any buttons, links, icons, etc with the cursor tip in the center of the element. Don't click boxes on their edges unless asked.

action.description:
The action to perform:
* `left_click`: Click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `right_click`: Click the right mouse button at the specified coordinates to open context menus.
* `double_click`: Double-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `triple_click`: Triple-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `type`: Type a string of text.
* `screenshot`: Take a screenshot of the screen.
* `wait`: Wait for a specified number of seconds.
* `scroll`: Scroll up, down, left, or right at the specified coordinates.
* `key`: Press a specific keyboard key.
* `left_click_drag`: Drag from start_coordinate to coordinate.
* `zoom`: Take a screenshot of a specific region for closer inspection.
* `scroll_to`: Scroll an element into view using its element reference ID from read_page or find tools.
* `hover`: Move the mouse cursor to the specified coordinates or element without clicking. Useful for revealing tooltips, dropdown menus, or triggering hover states.

coordinate.description: (x, y): The x (pixels from the left edge) and y (pixels from the top edge) coordinates. Required for `left_click`, `right_click`, `double_click`, `triple_click`, and `scroll`. For `left_click_drag`, this is the end position.

text.description: The text to type (for `type` action) or the key(s) to press (for `key` action). For `key` action: Provide space-separated keys (e.g., "Backspace Backspace Delete"). Supports keyboard shortcuts using the platform's modifier key (use "cmd" on Mac, "ctrl" on Windows/Linux, e.g., "cmd+a" or "ctrl+a" for select all). Page zoom shortcuts (e.g. "cmd+=", "ctrl+-", "cmd+0") are not supported and will return an error - use the `zoom` action to magnify a region of the page instead.

duration.description: The number of seconds to wait. Required for `wait`. Maximum 10 seconds.

scroll_direction.description: The direction to scroll. Required for `scroll`.

scroll_amount.description: The number of scroll wheel ticks. Optional for `scroll`, defaults to 3.

region.description: (x0, y0, x1, y1): The rectangular region to capture for `zoom`. Coordinates define a rectangle from top-left (x0, y0) to bottom-right (x1, y1) in pixels from the viewport origin. Required for `zoom` action. Useful for inspecting small UI elements like icons, buttons, or text.

scale.description: For `screenshot` and `zoom` only. Scale factor in [0.1, 1] for the returned image; 1 (default) uses the full image token budget, 0.5 returns an image at half the width and height (~quarter of the tokens). Coordinates are ALWAYS in the full-resolution coordinate frame (reported with every scaled screenshot), never in the scaled image's own pixels. Requires a Claude in Chrome extension version that supports scale; older extensions return the full-size image.

repeat.description: Number of times to repeat the key sequence. Only applicable for `key` action. Must be a positive integer between 1 and 100. Default is 1. Useful for navigation tasks like pressing arrow keys multiple times.

ref.description: Element reference ID from read_page or find tools (e.g., "ref_1", "ref_2"). Required for `scroll_to` action. Can be used as alternative to `coordinate` for click actions.

modifiers.description: Modifier keys for click actions. Supports: "ctrl", "shift", "alt", "cmd" (or "meta"), "win" (or "windows"). Can be combined with "+" (e.g., "ctrl+shift", "cmd+alt"). Optional.

tabId.description: Tab ID to execute the action on. Must be a tab in the current group. Use tabs_context_mcp first if you don't have a valid tab ID.

save_to_disk.description: For screenshot/zoom actions: save the image to disk so it can be attached to a message for the user. Returns the saved path in the tool result. Only set this when you intend to share the image — screenshots you're just looking at don't need saving.

action_summary.description: A few words saying what this action does on the page and to what, for example 'Sends the drafted reply to pat@example.com' or 'Opens the Filters menu'. Set it on every left_click, right_click, double_click, triple_click, left_click_drag, key and type action. State the effect only, and accurately: no reasons, nothing about what you were asked or allowed to do, no passwords or other secrets.

tools.name: mcp__claude-in-chrome__find

content.text:
Reports and their chats are now saved to Supabase, and it has already worked once on its own: your app saved `a20261108-053845-9b1fc4` at 05:55, with its PDF and all 8 drugs.

**Your question about the chat:** before this change, no. The chat lived only in the page and was lost on a reload, because the backend keeps no history. Now each report's conversation is saved with it, after every answer, and comes back when you reopen that report. Answers still being written aren't saved.

**What's stored, in the Supabase project the app already uses:**
- **Table `public.reports`:** one row per finished live run. It holds the run ids, the patient, a title, the summary, the ranked drugs (score and verdict), the full report data and the chat history.
- **Private bucket `reports`:** the PDF, at `<your user id>/<run id>.pdf`.
- **Access:** each row and PDF is visible only to its owner. I checked this in the database in a transaction I rolled back: as you, saving and reading a report and its chat worked; as a different signed-in user, nothing was visible and editing changed nothing.

**When it saves:** automatically when a live run finishes, and again harmlessly if a finished run is resumed after a reload. The report page shows "✓ Saved to your reports", "Not saved: sign in to keep reports", or the error. Signed out, nothing is saved and everything else works as before.

**Where you see them:** the Runs page now starts with **Saved reports**, read from Supabase, so they show up on any machine you sign in on. Each one has:
- **Open PDF:** works from anywhere.
- **Open in workspace:** replays the whole pipeline with its saved chat. This needs the backend that ran it, since the step-by-step history is still only in that machine's `backend/agent/runs/` folder. On another machine, use Open PDF.

**Checks:** the TypeScript check and production build pass, and Supabase's security check found nothing new (only an unrelated, pre-existing sign-in setting). I haven't clicked through these screens in the browser myself.

**Files:**
- New: `frontend/src/lib/reports-db.ts`, `frontend/src/components/discovery/saved-reports.tsx`, and the schema in `frontend/supabase/migrations/20261108105446_reports_and_chat.sql`. I created the table and bucket directly in your Supabase project; the file keeps the schema reproducible.

7 pages
RESEARCH REPORT · PATIENT-SPECIFIC ANALYSIS
Patient-specific drug repurposing candidates for limb-onset
amyotrophic lateral sclerosis: a multi-agent knowledge-graph and
literature analysis
Addo Labs
Addo Labs, ALS drug-repurposing pipeline · Report a20261108-053845-9b1fc4 · 8 November 2026
Abstract
Poorly BBB-penetrant drugs paired with MRgFUS were the delivery rationale. The BBB is a bottleneck for
most CNS drugs [1], and MRgFUS BBB opening has been shown feasible in ALS motor cortex [2] and as a
drug-delivery  approach  [3].  Candidates  came  from  knowledge-graph  target  links  [4]  across  the  patient's
profiles. None of the eight drugs is a classic large or efflux-limited molecule, so delivery gain was modest
overall. Ulimorelin (a 539 Da macrocyclic peptidomimetic with unknown CNS exposure) and CX717 (a novel
ampakine, never tested in ALS) scored highest because they are novel. Ezogabine has human ALS excitability
data [5] but carries QT, retinal and dependence risks, and it is a tested_in_als drug. Talampanel failed in ALS
[6]. Zonisamide is contraindicated by the sulfonamide allergy. P-chlorophenol is a toxic uncoupler and was
excluded. Evidence for the top picks is mechanistic only, so none is a clinical recommendation.
Keywords: amyotrophic lateral sclerosis; drug repurposing; knowledge graph; DRKG; focused ultrasound; blood–brain
barrier; multi-agent systems

    pdf.font(9.5)
    pdf.multi_cell(0, 4.8, f"**{pdf.t('Keywords:')}** {pdf.t(KEYWORDS)}", markdown=True)
    pdf.ln(2)
    pdf.rule(1)

    # --------------------------------------------------------------- 1 introduction
    pdf.section("1. Introduction")
    pdf.para("Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) is a progressive neurodegenerative disease of upper and lower motor neurons. "
             "Approved disease-modifying treatments are few and their benefit is modest, and the disease is heterogeneous in "
             "onset, genetics and rate of progression, so a single treatment strategy rarely fits every patient. Repurposing drugs "
             "that are already approved or clinically characterised can shorten the path to testing, but many candidate compounds "
             "reach the central nervous system poorly because of the blood–brain barrier (BBB).")
    pdf.para("Magnetic resonance-guided focused ultrasound (MRgFUS) can open the BBB transiently and locally, which may widen the "
             "set of compounds worth considering to include those that do not cross it unaided. This report applies an automated, "
             "patient-specific pipeline to one patient: it derives the therapeutic profiles that matter for this case, retrieves "
             "matching compounds from a biomedical knowledge graph, and assesses each against the literature and the patient's "
             "record. Its purpose is hypothesis generation for discussion with the care team.")

    # ----------------------------------------------------------------- 2 background
    pdf.section("2. Background")

**2. One list, no separate "Saved reports" section.** The page is now a single grid:
- **Signed in:** your reports saved in Supabase, from any machine, followed by any simulated runs from this session (those are never saved, and are marked "Simulated").

**3. Introduction". Simulated runs get the same layout, with text from their top candidate.

**4. PDF file name.** Downloads are now named **`Alex Moreau (alex).pdf`**: the patient's name and their patient id. That's the record id `alex`, not the run id, which is still printed inside the PDF.

**Not changed:** the *simulated* report PDF (`frontend/src/lib/report-pdf.ts`) still uses the old layout. Say if you want it restyled to match the paper too. I also removed the now-unused `saved-reports.tsx`.

content.text:
Live runs now use the case PDF you upload instead of the built-in record, so the patient will no longer be "Alex Moreau". Before this, the agent always planned from a separate, hand-written record named Alex Moreau, and that's where the name came from.

**What happens when you press Run:**
1. Your PDF goes to the backend, and Claude reads it into a patient record. The step shows in the analysis trace as `ingest_case_pdf`, with what it found ("4 medications, 6 lab results, …").
2. The record is saved under the patient's name plus a fingerprint of the file, e.g. `alex-chen-d1cb54`. Running the same PDF again reuses the record instead of reading it again.
3. Every stage then uses that record. The research agents, the drug assessment, the PDF's patient name and its file name now all match your upload: `Alex Chen (alex-chen-d1cb54).pdf`.

**Tested:** I posted the repo's synthetic sample chart through the same path. The record was built in 9 s and named after the chart's patient ("Jordan Ellis"), and I deleted the test record afterwards. The TypeScript check and production build pass. I haven't run a full pipeline from the browser with this, so your next live run is the first real test. Restart :8001 first.

**Privacy changes that came with this:**
- **Upload page wording.** It used to say "Stays in your browser". It now says the PDF is sent to Claude when the pipeline runs live, and to use synthetic or de-identified cases only.
- **Uploaded records stay out of git.** The backend saves them in a folder the repo tracks, so I added a gitignore rule; only the two sample patients stay tracked.

**Reports cards.** The "Top: … · Worth discussing · 55/100" line is gone. Each card now shows just the file name and when it was created, under the paper preview, with the download button.

**One leftover:** the report already saved to Supabase was generated from the old record, so it still says Alex Moreau. Delete it and re-run for a clean Alex Chen report, or tell me and I'll delete that row and its PDF.

content.text:
Clicking a report card now opens the PDF in the app's own viewer, a panel that slides in from the right, and nothing on the Reports page sends you back into the pipeline. The TypeScript check and production build pass, but I haven't opened a report in the browser. Also untested: that a saved PDF displays inside the panel rather than downloading; Supabase normally displays files unless asked to download, so test one before the demo.

**Where each PDF comes from now:**
- **Saved reports (signed in):** straight from Supabase storage via a short-lived private link. They keep working with the agent backend switched off, from any machine.
- **Simulated runs:** rebuilt in the browser, so no backend is needed.
- **Live runs from a signed-out session:** never saved, so their PDF still lives on the backend. If it's gone, the viewer says so plainly ("never saved, and the agent backend that made it no longer has it") instead of breaking. A card with no PDF at all is greyed out and marked "PDF unavailable".

**The viewer:**
- **Header:** the file name (`Alex Chen (alex-chen-d1cb54).pdf`) and creation date, plus a **Download** button that saves under that same name.
- **Body:** the browser's own PDF viewer, so zoom, search and paging work as usual.
- **Closing:** Escape, the close button or a click outside, with keyboard focus kept inside the panel while it's open.

**Removed:** "Open in workspace", and the store action behind it, now unused. Reloading mid-run still resumes as before; only the Reports page stopped depending on the backend.

**One side effect:** you can no longer go from a saved report back to its chat. The chat history is still saved in Supabase with each report. If you want it, I can show it read-only in the viewer next to the PDF.

`docs/STATUS.md` is updated to match. Everything is still uncommitted.

"""Launch the local facial, speech and tracing tests in one browser session."""
import argparse
import errno
import json
import subprocess
import threading
import time
import webbrowser
from http.server import BaseHTTPRequestHandler, ThreadingHTTPServer
from pathlib import Path
from urllib.request import urlopen
from urllib.error import URLError

APP = Path(__file__).resolve().parent
ROOT = APP.parent
URL = "http://127.0.0.1:8772"
SERVICES = {
    "facial": ("facial-test", "app.py", 8771, b"poster-expression-challenge-v1"),
    "speech": ("speech-test-good", "transcript_only.py", 8770, b"transcript-only-v1"),
}
CHILDREN = {}
LOCK = threading.Lock()


def healthy(url, expected):
    try:
        with urlopen(url + "/health", timeout=1) as response:
            if response.read(128) != expected:
                raise RuntimeError("A different app is using " + url)
            return True
    except URLError as error:
        if getattr(error.reason, "errno", None) in (errno.ECONNREFUSED,):
            return False
        raise RuntimeError("Could not reach the test at " + url) from error


def start_test(stage):
    if stage == "line":
        return "/trace"
    directory, script, port, signature = SERVICES[stage]
    url = f"http://127.0.0.1:{port}"
    with LOCK:
        if healthy(url, signature):
            return url
        folder = ROOT / directory
        python = folder / ".venv/bin/python"
        if not python.is_file():
            raise RuntimeError(f"Run setup.sh in {directory} first.")
        process = CHILDREN.get(stage)
        if process is None or process.poll() is not None:
            process = subprocess.Popen([str(python), "-B", script, "--no-browser"], cwd=folder)
            CHILDREN[stage] = process
        deadline = time.monotonic()+90
        while time.monotonic()<deadline:
            if process.poll() is not None:
                raise RuntimeError(f"{directory} could not start. Check the launcher terminal.")
            try:
                if healthy(url, signature):
                    return url
            except RuntimeError:
                pass  # Model initialization may have bound the port already.
            time.sleep(.25)
        raise RuntimeError("Test startup is taking longer than expected. Try Begin again.")

        self.send_header("Cache-Control","no-store")
        self.end_headers()

questions.question: The take-home test's facial check already has a pass rule (top prediction matches the expression and confidence ≥ 80%). content.text:
I've built the take-home test feature. There's a new **Take-home test** tab, the test sends its results back to the web app when it's done, a one-page PDF report is made from them, and it's saved to Supabase and shown under Reports → **Test results**. I couldn't run the full flow on this machine, because the camera and microphone tests aren't set up here.

**The tab** (sidebar → Library → Take-home test):
- A short list of the three tasks: facial expressions, passage reading and line tracing.
- **Open the take-home test**, which opens the test app in its own window.
- A live check of whether the test app is running on this computer, and the command to start it if not.

**What happens when you finish the test:**
1. The test window sends its scores back to the Addo Labs tab that opened it, and only to that tab's address, since these are health measurements. You can be on any page of the app; it doesn't have to be the Take-home tab.
2. The app scores the results, builds the PDF and saves it to your account.
3. It appears on the Reports page under its own **Test results** heading, which reads "Take-home test results only. These are not drug-repurposing reports." Clicking a card opens the PDF in the viewer.
4. If the app tab was closed during the test, the test's last screen offers a results file, and the Take-home tab has **Import results file** for it.

**The report**, one clean page:
- An overview table with accuracy, number passed and pass rate for each of the three tests.
- One small table per test, with each item's score and PASS or FAIL written out.
- Each test's pass rule, and a line saying it's a screening aid, not a diagnosis.

The pass rules: facial uses the test's own rule (top prediction is the requested expression, at ≥ 80%). Speech passes at ≥ 90% of words read correctly per passage, and tracing at ≥ 80% of the line inside the guide per shape, as you chose.

**What I tested:**
- **Report logic:** a realistic set of results through the real scoring and PDF code. The PDF's numbers match a hand calculation, and its PASS/FAIL rows are right.
- **Test app server:** started it here; the routes it serves work.
- **Builds:** the TypeScript check and production build pass.

**Not tested, needs a set-up machine:** a full real run, from opening the test through results arriving and being saved. The facial and speech tests need their `setup.sh` (PyTorch and model downloads, macOS-oriented); neither is set up here, so only line tracing can run on this machine. Do one full run on the demo laptop before the expo.

**Other changes, outside the web app:**
- **The three tests** now include their structured scores in the "done" message they already sent, alongside the text summary. These are small additive edits to their files.
- **Two Windows bugs in the test launcher, fixed.** It looked for Python only in the macOS location, and it treated "server not started yet" as a fatal error on Windows. It also rejected the page address the new tab uses.
- **Supabase:** reports now have a `kind` column (drug assessment or take-home test). It's applied to your project, with the SQL in `frontend/supabase/migrations/`.
- **Naming:** the sidebar's "Runs & reports" is now **Reports**, to match the page title.
- **Docs:** the new optional `VITE_TAKE_HOME_URL` setting is in `frontend/.env.example`, and the feature is logged in `docs/STATUS.md`.

Everything is uncommitted.

content.text:
It's spread across the test app (backend) and the web app (frontend):

**The take-home test app** (`backend/diagnostics/`), which sends its results back:

| File | What it does |
|---|---|
| `master-app/diagnostic-ui/suite.js` | Collects each test's results; at **Complete Diagnostic** sends them to the Addo Labs tab that opened it, or offers the results file |
| `master-app/diagnostic-ui/index.html` | The "results sent" message and the download link on the final screen |
| `master-app/diagnostic_complete.py` | The launcher: the Windows fixes, and accepting the `?return=` address |
| `facial-test/round.js` | Adds each expression's confidence, top prediction and pass to its "done" message |
| `speech-test-good/transcript_only.html` | Adds each passage's word and error counts to its "done" message |
| `line-test/index.html` | Adds each shape's accuracy and time to its "done" message |

**The web app** (`frontend/src/`):

| File | What it does |
|---|---|
| `components/take-home-page.tsx` | The **Take-home test** tab: task list, open button, test-app status, latest results table, file import |
| `lib/take-home-store.tsx` | Receives results from the test window (on any page), names them after the patient, and saves them |
| `lib/take-home.ts` | Checks the results, applies the pass rules (`SPEECH_PASS = 90`, `LINE_PASS = 80`), and builds the PDF (`buildTestPdf`) |
| `lib/reports-db.ts` | `saveTestReport()` writes the PDF and row to Supabase; `listReports('take_home_test')` reads them back |
| `components/discovery/runs.tsx` | The Reports page: the **Test results** section, its card thumbnail, and the PDF viewer |
| `components/app-sidebar.tsx` | The **Take-home test** sidebar entry |
| `pages/Home.tsx` | Mounts the results listener and routes `/home/take-home` to the tab |

**Database:** `frontend/supabase/migrations/20261108120606_reports_kind_take_home_test.sql` adds the `kind` column (already applied to your Supabase project).

**Docs:** `frontend/.env.example` (the optional `VITE_TAKE_HOME_URL` setting) and the "Take-home test → report" entry in `docs/STATUS.md`.

The take-home test now saves its own results to the same Supabase project as the rest of the app, and the web app only gives you the link and shows the results. I checked the saving step against your live database, but I haven't run a full test in the browser: the facial and speech tests aren't set up on this machine.

**How it works now:**
1. **The link.** On the Take-home test tab, **Open the take-home test** opens it, and **Copy test link** copies it so you can send it to a patient. Each link is new, works once, and expires after 7 days.
2. **What's in the link.** A one-time code tied to your account, plus the project's public address and key, which are already public in the web app. They sit in the part of the address browsers never send to the test server.
3. **Saving.** When all three tests are done, the test sends its results straight to Supabase, so it doesn't need a sign-in and the web-app tab doesn't need to stay open. Its last screen confirms "Your results were saved to Addo Labs."
4. **Showing them.** The tab picks the results up within a few seconds and shows the summary table. They also appear under Reports → **Test results**, and clicking one opens its PDF. Only the results are stored; the PDF is drawn from them whenever it's opened.
5. **The fallback.** A test opened *without* an Addo Labs link can't save. It says so and offers a results file to import on the tab instead.

**What I checked against your real database** (the test data is deleted again):
- Submitting results the exact way the test app does, with only the public key and no sign-in, filed a report under the account that made the link.
- Reusing the link was rejected, with the readable message the test shows.
- The test app's address is allowed to call Supabase from a browser.
- In a separate rolled-back test: an unknown code was rejected, and someone with no account could read no reports or links.

**The security warning in Supabase.** Its security check now flags the saving function as "callable without signing in". That's intentional: the test has no sign-in, so the one-time code is the permission. The function can only file one results report for that code's owner, and does nothing else. I've noted this in the migration file so nobody "fixes" it later.

**What changed:**
- **Test app:** `backend/diagnostics/master-app/diagnostic-ui/suite.js` now does the saving. The earlier step that sent results back to the app tab is removed.
- **Database:** the one-time links table and the saving function are applied to your project, with the SQL in `frontend/supabase/migrations/20261108122113_take_home_invites_and_submit.sql`.
- **Web app:** the Take-home tab, the Reports page and the store code are updated, and I removed leftovers from the old flow.
- **Checks:** the TypeScript check and production build pass, and `docs/STATUS.md` is updated.

The test app still runs locally on :8772 alongside the main app, so a link only opens on a computer that's running it. If you meant patients should be able to take it from their own computers, the test pages would need to be hosted online; the saving already works from anywhere.

content.text:
You're half right. The suite page and the line-tracing test are plain HTML, but nothing is serving them right now, and two of the three tests can't work as plain HTML at all.

**Why the link fails:**
1. **Nothing is running on this computer at that address.** The link points to `http://127.0.0.1:8772`, which is served by a small Python program (`diagnostic_complete.py`), and it isn't running; ports 8770, 8771 and 8772 are all empty. So the browser finds no site there.
2. **`127.0.0.1` means "this computer".** A copied link opened on someone else's laptop looks for the test on *their* machine, not yours. So even with the program running, a link sent to a patient only works if they have the repo and the test running themselves.

**Why it can't simply be static HTML:**

| Test | What its page needs |
|---|---|
| Line tracing | Nothing; it's pure browser code and works as a static file |
| Facial expressions | Posts each photo to `/photo` on a local Python server (port 8771), which runs the POSTER++ emotion model in PyTorch |
| Passage reading | Posts the recording to `/score` on a local Python server (port 8770), which runs the Vosk speech recogniser |

Those two servers also aren't set up on this machine; each needs its `setup.sh` first, which installs PyTorch and Vosk and downloads the models.

**Ways forward:**
1. **For the demo, on one machine:** run the setups once, then `python backend/diagnostics/master-app/diagnostic_complete.py`, and the link works on that computer. I can try the setups here on Windows. The scripts are written for macOS, and they download PyTorch plus about 40 MB of speech model, so I'd confirm the download with you before starting.
2. **Make the link work anywhere:** move the test pages into the web app so they're served with it, and replace the two Python models with in-browser versions: an emotion model running in the browser (ONNX), and the browser's own speech recognition or a WebAssembly Vosk. Then it really is "just HTML", and a link sent to a patient works on their own device. This is the right design for a true take-home test, but it's a few hours of work and changes how the facial and speech tests score, so their accuracy would need re-checking.
3. **Quick middle step:** serve the suite and the line-tracing test from the web app now, so the link always opens, and show the facial and speech tests as "needs the local test app" until option 2 is done.

With the deadline close, I'd do option 1 for the demo and mention option 2 as the next step. Which do you want?

content.text:
Deploying as-is would **not** work, and a child route under Addo Labs is the right design. Here's why, then what I'd recommend.

**What breaks if you deploy the current setup:**
1. **Hard-coded local addresses.** The test link is `http://127.0.0.1:8772`. The three test pages also only send their results to `http://127.0.0.1:8772`, and the launcher rejects any other address.
2. **Two separate Python servers.** The facial test (PyTorch emotion model) and the speech test (Vosk recogniser) each run their own server on this machine, started by a third program, the launcher. Deploying means hosting all three.
3. **Camera and microphone need HTTPS.** Browsers only grant them on `https://` sites or on `localhost`. A deployed test must be served over HTTPS, and the launcher is plain HTTP.
4. **The pipeline has the same problem.** The web app finds the agent backend at `127.0.0.1:8001`, and that backend only accepts requests from `localhost`. - **Links work on any device.** A link sent to a patient opens on their phone or laptop, and they don't need the repo.
- **The two models, by folding them into the existing FastAPI backend.** Add two endpoints next to the agent's (`/api/diagnostics/photo` and `/api/diagnostics/score`) that run the same PyTorch and Vosk code as today. Scoring stays identical, and it's the "same backend as this repo" you asked for earlier. The alternative is in-browser models (an ONNX emotion model, and browser speech recognition or WebAssembly Vosk), which needs no backend for the test at all. But the scores would change, and the accuracy would need re-checking.

input.content:
# Deploying Addo Labs: Vercel (frontend) + Vultr (backend)

```
browser ──https──► Vercel: frontend/ (the app, plus the take-home test at /take-home/)
   │                    │
   │                    └── Supabase (auth, reports, take-home results): called directly by the browser
   └──https──► Vultr: backend/ (FastAPI, :8001 behind Caddy)
                 /api/research · /api/drkg · /api/assess   the discovery pipeline
                 /api/diagnostics/{facial,speech}          take-home test scoring
```

Everything below was written on 2026-11-08 and checked locally, not against a live deploy.
Do one full run on the deployed site before relying on it.

## 1. Backend on Vultr

Ubuntu 24.04, at least 4 GB RAM (PyTorch + the POSTER++ model + DRKG). No GPU needed.

```bash
sudo apt update && sudo apt install -y python3-venv git unzip curl caddy
git clone <repo> addo && cd addo/backend
python3 -m venv .venv
.venv/bin/pip install -r agent/requirements.txt -r diagnostics/requirements.txt \
    --extra-index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cpu
cp agent/.env.example agent/.env      # fill in ANTHROPIC_API_KEY etc., and:
#   AGENT_CORS_ORIGINS=https://<your-app>.vercel.app   (and any custom domain)
```

**Take-home test models** (the scripts also make their own small venvs; harmless):

```bash
bash diagnostics/facial-test/setup.sh          # POSTER++ checkpoint + face detector → facial-test/assets/
bash diagnostics/speech-test-good/setup.sh     # Vosk model → speech-test-good/private/speech_demo/
```

The speech script's last step (`make_samples.py`, reference voices) uses macOS `say` and fails on
Linux; that only removes the "play the reference" button on the review screen. Scoring works.
Check with `curl localhost:8001/api/diagnostics/health` once the API runs: both should be `true`.

**DRKG data** (stage 3), 217 MB, into `backend/.venv/data/drkg/`: the commands are in
`agent/.env.example` under "Stage 3".

**Run it** as a service (`/etc/systemd/system/addo-api.service`):

```ini
[Service]
WorkingDirectory=/home/<user>/addo/backend
ExecStart=/home/<user>/addo/backend/.venv/bin/python -m agent.api
Restart=always
User=<user>
[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target
```

It binds `127.0.0.1:8001` only. **Never `uvicorn --reload`** (breaks the agent's subprocesses).

**HTTPS with Caddy** (`/etc/caddy/Caddyfile`); point a DNS A record at the server first:

```
api.<your-domain> {
    reverse_proxy 127.0.0.1:8001
}
```

`sudo systemctl enable --now addo-api caddy`. Caddy gets the certificate itself. HTTPS is not
optional: the Vercel site is HTTPS, and browsers block calls from it to an `http://` backend.

## 2. Frontend on Vercel

- **Root directory:** `frontend` · framework Vite · build `npm run build` · output `dist`.
- **Environment variables:** `VITE_SUPABASE_URL`, `VITE_SUPABASE_ANON_KEY`,
  `VITE_AGENT_URL=https://api.<your-domain>`. Leave `VITE_TAKE_HOME_URL` unset.
- `frontend/vercel.json` rewrites app routes (`/home/...`) to the SPA, so reloading a page works;
  real files, including `/take-home/`, are served first.

## 3. Supabase

- **Auth → URL configuration:** add `https://<your-app>.vercel.app/home` (and custom domains) to the
  redirect URLs, and set the site URL, or Google sign-in returns to localhost.
- The schema is already applied; it's recorded in `frontend/supabase/migrations/`.

## The take-home test

`https://<your-app>/take-home/index.html`, opened from the app's **Take-home test** tab (or a copied
link). The link carries a one-time code; on completion the test saves results straight to Supabase
(`submit_take_home`), so it works on any device, signed in or not. The pages are copies of
`backend/diagnostics/*`: after editing those, run `npm run sync:take-home` in `frontend/` and
commit `frontend/public/take-home/`. Locally, the original launcher still works
(`python backend/diagnostics/master-app/diagnostic_complete.py`).

# Environment update
 - Primary working directory: C:\Users\jerem\BioHacks-2026\backend\diagnostics\master-app (was C:\Users\jerem\BioHacks-2026)

The take-home test now lives inside the Addo Labs site at **`/take-home/`**, so it deploys to Vercel with the frontend, and its facial and speech scoring is part of the existing backend for Vultr. I tested each piece locally; nothing has been tried on a real Vercel or Vultr deploy, and no test has been taken end to end in a browser.

**How it fits together once deployed:**

| Piece | Where it runs |
|---|---|
| The app, plus the test pages at `https://<your-app>/take-home/index.html` | Vercel, over HTTPS, so camera and microphone work |
| Facial and speech scoring, at `/api/diagnostics` on the same FastAPI backend | Vultr |
| Line tracing | Entirely in the browser |
| Test results (one-time link, saved by the test itself) | Supabase, unchanged |

A link opens on any device; the patient doesn't need the repo or a local server.

**What I built:**
- **One copy of each test page.** The pages in `backend/diagnostics/` stay the originals, and `npm run sync:take-home` (in `frontend/`) copies them into `frontend/public/take-home/`. The copies are committed and marked "generated", so Vercel needs neither Python nor anything outside `frontend/`. Re-run the sync after editing a test page.
- **The same pages work locally and deployed.** They read the scoring server's address from their link and default to the old local servers, so the local launcher still works as before.
- **Scoring on the backend** (`backend/diagnostics/api.py`). It runs the exact same facial (PyTorch) and speech (Vosk) code as before, so scores are unchanged. Until the models are installed on the server it answers "not installed", and the rest of the API is unaffected.
- **Production settings:** the backend now accepts your deployed site through `AGENT_CORS_ORIGINS`, which is required in production. The Take-home tab checks whether the server can score the facial and speech tests and says so.

**Fixes found along the way:**
- **Page reloads on Vercel.** There was no Vercel config, so reloading any `/home/...` page would have shown a 404. `frontend/vercel.json` fixes that.
- **Package conflict on the server.** The facial model needs `numpy<2.1` but the DRKG step pinned `2.5.4`, so they couldn't share a server environment. I relaxed the DRKG pin to `numpy>=2.0`; the DRKG code works on 2.0.x. I didn't run a full combined install to confirm, because it would download PyTorch.

**What I checked locally:**
- **Pages served:** your dev server returns all six test pages at their new addresses, and the production build includes them.
- **Scoring API:** it answers correctly without the models installed (a clear 503), accepts the local and configured production sites, and refuses others.
- **Nothing else broken:** the agent API's other routes and the 12 backend tests pass, the local launcher still works, and the TypeScript check passes.

**Deployment guide: `docs/DEPLOY.md`.** It's step by step:
- **Vultr:** server size, install commands, the two model setup scripts, a systemd service, and Caddy for automatic HTTPS (required, because browsers block an HTTPS site calling an `http://` backend).
- **Vercel:** root directory `frontend`, plus `VITE_AGENT_URL` set to the backend's HTTPS address.
- **Supabase:** add the production URL to Google sign-in's allowed redirects, or sign-in will send people back to localhost.

**Two gaps:**
- **Reference voices on Linux.** The speech test's "play the reference voice" files are made with macOS `say`, so on the Vultr server that button won't have audio. Scoring isn't affected.
- **Your local :8001 backend** is still running old code. Restart it to get `/api/diagnostics`.

Everything is uncommitted. `AGENTS.md` and `docs/STATUS.md` are updated to match.
